subtitle: Dodona and Delphi give one answer: the gods sent the wolves, and Euenius must have whatever recompense he chooses

notes.label: Pairing
notes.quote: ἔν τε Δωδώνῃ καὶ ἐν Δελφοῖς
notes.body: The two greatest oracles of mainland Greece are linked by τε καί, so their shared answer carries huge authority.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The subject is held back until after the verb, so the reader's attention falls on who is speaking: the gods themselves.

notes.label: Direct speech
notes.body: The gods speak in their own words, so the reader hears their verdict directly, which makes it more powerful.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: "Unjustly" is the first word of the reply, so the gods condemn the Apollonians' court before they explain anything.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.trans: the guardian of the sacred sheep
notes.body: The gods give Euenius his title, which reminds the Apollonians that he was serving the gods.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The pronoun is not needed with the verb, so it stresses that it was the gods themselves who sent the wolves.

notes.label: Irony
notes.trans: we set the wolves on them
notes.body: The wolves were sent by the gods, so Euenius was blinded for something the gods themselves did.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: The strong negative shows that the punishment will not stop until the Apollonians obey, so they have no room to bargain.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Αὐτός makes clear that Euenius alone decides his compensation, with no one else involved.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two verbs together give Euenius full control, which makes him the judge of what is fair.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.trans: you give … we will give a gift
notes.body: Words for giving are repeated, so the reader sees a fair exchange: first the Apollonians must give, then the gods will.

notes.label: Parallelism
notes.body: Euenius himself will choose and the gods themselves will give, which makes both sides of the settlement personal.

notes.label: Foreshadowing
notes.trans: a gift such that … they will call him blessed
notes.body: The gift is not named, only its effect, so the reader is left wondering what it will be until the end of the story.

notes.label: Dodona
notes.body: An oracle of Zeus in Epirus, in north-west Greece, believed to be the oldest in the Greek world. It was associated with a sacred oak, and thousands of lead tablets inscribed with visitors' questions have been found there.

notes.label: Delphi
notes.body: Apollo's oracle on the slopes of Mount Parnassus above the Gulf of Corinth, where the god spoke through his priestess, the Pythia. It was consulted by cities and individuals from all over the Greek world.

questions: What does the gods' reply show about how they judged Euenius, and how they judged the Apollonians?
Why do you think the gods insist that Euenius should choose his own recompense?
What is the effect of leaving the gods' promised gift unexplained?

context.body: When a Greek community met a disaster it could not explain, such as plague, failed harvests or barren flocks, it commonly sent to an oracle to ask which god was angry and what would put things right. Delphi, Apollo's sanctuary on the slopes of Mount Parnassus, was the most prestigious: there the god answered through his priestess, the Pythia. Dodona, in Epirus in north-west Greece, was an oracle of Zeus, said to be the oldest in Greece, where the god's will was linked with a sacred oak. Excavators there have found thousands of small lead tablets on which ordinary people scratched their questions: about marriages, journeys, illnesses and lost property, as well as the affairs of cities. Consulting two oracles and getting the same answer from both left the Apollonians in no doubt.
